newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia media, politicians attack Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia media, politicians attack Singapore.

text.p: Malaysian newspapers and politicians on Thursday launched a retaliatory attack on Singapore, quoting a United Nations report as saying the island nation had more crime than its neighbour.

A report in the daily New Straits Times said there were more homicides, assaults and robberies in Singapore than in Malaysia. It was an obvious response to a Singapore newspaper report of high crime levels in Malaysia's southern Johor state.

"The crime rate in Singapore is higher than in Malaysia, according to the United Nations Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice's latest report," the New Straits Times said in a front page report from Johor Baru, the capital of Johor state.
Singapore's Straits Times this week published stories saying former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew was justified in his remarks about violent crime in Johor.

Lee's remarks that Johor was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings" were made in a court affidavit in a libel suit against a Singapore opposition politician, sparking a major row between the two neighbours.

Malaysia reacted with fury to what it perceived as a major insult. Lee, in a rare move, offered an unreserved apology and on his request the Singapore High Court on Monday ordered the remarks deleted from the affidavit.
In a statement on Thursday, the opposition Parti Rakyat Malaysia said it wanted to draw attention to a U.N. report on crimes.

It quoted statistics from a lecture by Francis T. Seow, a visiting fellow on East Asia legal studies at Harvard Law School and a former solicitor-general in Singapore, to prove the higher crime rate in Singapore.

"According to the latest U.N. Commission on Justice on crime statistics worldwide, the homicide rate in Malaysia (1.76 per 100,000) is slightly lower than that of Singapore (1.77 per 100,000)," the political party said, quoting from Seow's speech titled: "The politics and judicial institutions in Singapore".
"But, the rate of assaults in Singapore (34.12 per 100,000) is more than twice that of Malaysia (14.54 per 100,000)," Seow said in the lecture at the University of Sydney two weeks ago.
It said the rate of robberies in Singapore, at 56.13 per 100,000 people, was also almost double Malaysia's 32.75.
On Wednesday, Malaysian cabinet ministers reacted angrily to the Singapore newspaper report, one even calling for a "media war".
"I call on the local media to take up the challenge," Minister for International and Industry Rafidah Aziz said.

"There are a lot of things the Malaysian media can write about Singapore. See what's happening in Singapore, the opposition is being killed... My advice to the Singapore media is to stop it or suffer the consequences for your country," she told reporters.
But, Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad chose not to fan the flames of the dispute. "I don't want to prolong the matter," he told reporters at a conference on Wednesday evening.
At the same conference, Education Minister Najib Tun Razak said he thought the Singapore Straits Times articles were officially inspired.
